Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.

=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter
Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and
non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.
Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public
registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the
Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or
public records.
Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)
will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.
Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing
bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds
flow.)
Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio
matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.
Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter
and is not expected to be material.
Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course
operating costs.
Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime
above.
Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.
Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and
records are fictional.
1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the
indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including
DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,
payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.
2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause
11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final
written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.
3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security
is included.
4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of
every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of
non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.
5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject
to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft
Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or
on-costs apply.
6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external
email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity
timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised
person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation
remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no
loss amount.
7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as
a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.
8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each
(AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether
each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.
9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale
consent is required merely because shares are sold.
10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of
the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the
Buyer has completed its own verification.
11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer
must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Basis:** Seller Update positions and Disclosure Letter only. I have not seen the full SPA mark-up, the data room documents (DD-002 to DD-012) or any W&I policy terms. Positions below are starting points for negotiation and should be checked against the full draft and diligence reports.

---

## 1. Headline view

The cover note calls this a "fair and balanced package". It is not.

The Seller's own Disclosure Letter contradicts several statements in its Update:
- Bluefen is "addressed", but the letter says there is no consent and no evidence the conditions are satisfied.
- Riverlark is "addressed", but the facility is not repaid and no discharge is provided.
- The DD-006 incident is "not expected to be material", but the letter says scope, access and notification are all unresolved.

The structure works against us in four ways at once:
1. General disclosure of the entire data room and public records.
2. An anti-sandbagging clause covering actual *and constructive* knowledge.
3. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applied to "all Claims of any nature".
4. Fundamental warranties pulled into the 20% cap and 18-month window.

Taken together, **every risk we have actually identified in diligence would be uncompensated.** We know about these risks, so the knowledge clause and general disclosure bar warranty claims. Any indemnity is then caps-limited, time-barred and shielded by non-reliance. Any W&I policy will also exclude known matters. This interaction is the central point to make in our response.

---

## 2. Structural and risk-allocation issues

### 2.1 Fundamental warranties in the general cap and time limit
**Seller position:** Capacity and title warranties are subject to the same 20% / 18-month regime "for administrative simplicity".

**Why it hurts us:** Title is the whole deal. If Harbourglass cannot pass clean title to 100% of the shares, our loss is up to the full AUD 24m, not AUD 4.8m. Eighteen months is far too short for title defects, which often surface only on a later refinancing or exit.

**Push back:**
- Fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority, solvency, capital structure, no encumbrances) should be capped at 100% of the price.
- Their time limit should be at least 6 to 7 years, aligned with NSW limitation periods for contract.
- They should be excluded from the de minimis and basket.
- "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to remove the core protection.

### 2.2 "Any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (cl 12.3/13)
**Why it hurts us:** This default rule silently sweeps the caps, thresholds and time limits into indemnities, the tax covenant, leakage or price-adjustment claims, and potentially fraud. It inverts the usual drafting burden, so every carve-out we fail to spell out is lost.

**Push back:**
- Reverse the default. Limitations should apply only to general Warranty Claims unless expressly extended.
- Expressly exclude fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment; specific indemnities; the tax covenant; leakage and price adjustment; and breaches of pre-Completion covenants.

### 2.3 Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applied to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)
**Why it hurts us:** This purports to cap or exclude claims for fraud and misleading or deceptive conduct, and to channel all relief into a capped warranty regime. Under NSW law, a party cannot contract out of liability for its own fraud. Non-reliance clauses are relevant to, but not necessarily decisive of, a claim under s 18 of the Australian Consumer Law. We should not rely on those doctrines, though, and should not accept drafting that invites argument.

**Push back:**
- Carve out fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment from all limitations, from exclusive remedy and from non-reliance. This should cover fraud by the Seller and by the Company's officers and Seller representatives acting before Completion.
- Preserve equitable remedies, including injunction and specific performance, and the right to terminate before Completion.
- Make non-reliance operate only in respect of statements *outside* the Warranties, Disclosure Letter and Transaction Documents.

### 2.4 Cap (20% / AUD 4.8m) and thresholds (AUD 25k de minimis; AUD 250k deductible basket)
**Why it hurts us:**
- The basket is a *deductible*. We absorb the first AUD 250k even when it is exceeded.
- There is no aggregation of related claims. This matters directly: the three Sandbar renewals of AUD 110k each, or a series of privacy-related claims, should be counted together.
- The 20% cap is within market range only if a W&I policy sits above it. If there is no W&I, it is light for a business with these known issues.

**Push back:**
- Make the basket a **tipping** basket, so that once it is exceeded the full amount is recoverable from the first dollar.
- Reduce the basket to around 0.5% of the price (AUD 120k) and the de minimis to around AUD 10k to 15k.
- Add an express rule that claims arising from the same or related facts aggregate for the de minimis.
- On the cap, confirm whether W&I is being placed:
  - If yes, we can trade on the general cap, but specific indemnities must sit outside the policy and the cap.
  - If no, seek 30% to 50% for general warranties.

### 2.5 General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Schedule 7; DL 1.1–1.2)
**Why it hurts us:** Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in" the data room shifts the whole diligence risk onto us. The words "referred to" also reach documents that are not even in the data room. Disclosing "publicly searchable corporate records" with no date or list is open-ended.

**Push back:**
- Delete general data room disclosure.
- Only matters **fairly disclosed** in the Disclosure Letter, with enough detail to let a buyer identify their nature, scope and financial effect, should qualify the Warranties.
- If any public records disclosure survives, limit it to specified ASIC and PPSR searches obtained on a stated date, with copies annexed.
- State that the Disclosure Letter does not qualify fundamental warranties, the tax covenant or specific indemnities.

### 2.6 Buyer knowledge / anti-sandbagging (cl 8.3)
**Why it hurts us:** It bars claims for anything we or our advisers "had knowledge" of, *including anything discoverable* from the data room or public records. This constructive-knowledge standard is the most damaging single clause. It would extinguish warranty claims for Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, DD-005, DD-006 and Sandbar, because each appears in the record.

**Push back:**
- Delete it.
- Replace with an express pro-sandbagging clause: the Buyer's rights are not affected by any investigation or knowledge, actual, constructive or imputed, other than matters fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter.
- At minimum, a fallback is the actual knowledge of named individuals, with no constructive knowledge and no adviser knowledge. That is still not ideal.

### 2.7 Disclosure Letter currency and updates
The Disclosure Letter speaks as at 22 September 2026, which is more than six weeks ago. Several matters, especially DD-006 and Bluefen, will have moved since.

**Push back:**
- The Seller must provide a current bring-down.
- Any update before Completion must not cure a breach of a Warranty repeated at Completion unless we consent.
- A material adverse update should give us a right to terminate.

---

## 3. Specific known-risk items

These matters are *known*. They therefore cannot be dealt with through warranties, given the knowledge clause and likely W&I exclusions. Each needs a condition, a completion deliverable, a price mechanism or a specific indemnity.

### 3.1 Bluefen change-control consent (DD-002; cl 3 / 6.3)
**Facts:** Bluefen generates about AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue, roughly 30%. Change of control requires consent under cl 11.2, subject to conditions in cl 11.3. There is no consent and no evidence the conditions are satisfied (DL 2).

**Seller position:** Reasonable endeavours; the condition is "satisfied" on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

**Why it hurts us:** Losing 30% of revenue would destroy much of the value we are paying for. A bare written consent that is itself conditional, or that imposes new terms such as repricing, a shorter term or extra termination rights, would satisfy the Seller's drafting but not protect us.

**Push back:**
- Make the condition precedent require a written, unconditional consent, or one on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably.
- Require evidence that all cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied, and a confirmation that no termination or variation right arises from the transaction.
- Make the condition waivable by the Buyer only.
- Raise the Seller's obligation to "all reasonable endeavours" or best endeavours. Give us rights to review and approve communications with Bluefen and to attend meetings.
- Include a sunset date with a Buyer termination right.
- Consider whether a price adjustment or earn-out is needed if Bluefen terminates or materially varies within an agreed period after Completion.

### 3.2 Riverlark facility of about AUD 3.2m (DD-003; cl 2 / 7)
**Facts:** The facility is outstanding, with a change-of-control provision at cl 8.1 and discharge at cl 9.2. It is not repaid and there is no discharge (DL 3).

**Seller position:** A release "to be provided following Completion".

**Why it hurts us:** The deal is debt-free/cash-free. A post-Completion release leaves security over the Company, and therefore over our asset, held by a lender we have no relationship with. The change of control may also trigger an event of default at Completion.

**Push back:**
- Treat the facility as Debt deducted from the price.
- Pay it directly from the Completion funds flow to Riverlark under a **payoff letter**. The letter should state the exact payout figure including interest, break costs and fees, and should be delivered before Completion.
- Make executed deeds of release and discharge, PPSR financing change statements and the return of title documents a Completion deliverable, not a post-Completion promise.
- Add an indemnity for any amount above the payoff figure.

### 3.3 DD-005 Completion bonuses of AUD 420k
**Facts:** Conditional Completion bonuses total AUD 420k. They are not in the funds flow, and the letter is silent on payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs (DL 5).

**Seller position:** A "matter for the Seller", not separately itemised.

**Why it hurts us:** These are liabilities of the Company triggered by the transaction. If the Seller does not pay them and they are not deducted, the Company, and in effect we, bear them after Completion. That is a leak from a debt-free/cash-free price. On-costs are likely to include PAYG withholding, payroll tax and probably superannuation guarantee, plus possibly workers' compensation premium, so the true cost is materially above AUD 420k.

**Push back:**
- Define these bonuses, together with all employer on-costs, as Transaction Costs or Debt deducted from the price.
- Show them as a separate line in the funds flow, paid through Company payroll at or immediately after Completion with correct withholding.
- Add an uncapped indemnity for any bonus or on-cost liability.
- Commercially, check whether the "continued employment" conditions create retention issues or claims if any recipient leaves.

### 3.4 Ironquay IP (DD-004, DD-010; cl 11.1)
**Facts:** Transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open. There is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment (DL 4).

**Seller position:** The existing indemnity, limited to the SOW3 payment, is adequate.

**Why it hurts us:** Until all fees are paid, the Company may not own IP that it presumably uses in its analytics product. Our exposure is not limited to AUD 180k. It includes infringement claims, loss of use, re-development cost and customer impact. The Seller's own letter also concedes the AUD 180k figure is not bank-verified, so the amount owed may differ.

**Push back:**
- Require, as a condition or Completion deliverable, either evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees (to be paid by the Seller or deducted from the price) or confirmation from Ironquay of the amount required.
- Require an executed **confirmatory IP assignment** from Ironquay of all SOW3 Project Materials.
- Expand the indemnity to cover all loss from any failure of the Company to own or have unrestricted use of the SOW3 materials, including third-party claims and remediation cost. It should sit outside the cap and thresholds.

### 3.5 DD-006 export / privacy incident
**Facts:** A download link was sent to an unintended external address. The file may contain about 1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, timestamps). Access, scope and notification requirements were undetermined as at 22 September. The letter does not characterise it as a confirmed breach.

**Seller position:** Preliminary and "not expected to be material".

**Why it hurts us:**
- Business contact details and activity data are still personal information under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth).
- Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must generally complete a reasonable assessment within 30 days. More than 30 days have passed since 22 September, so we need to know whether an assessment was completed and on what basis.
- If notification was required and not made, the Company has an ongoing regulatory compliance issue. Penalties under the amended Privacy Act can be significant.
- Customer contractual notification and indemnity obligations may also apply, including potentially to Bluefen.
- The Seller has no basis for its "not material" characterisation, and its own letter says the facts are not yet established.

**Push back:**
- Require an immediate update: forensic findings, whether the link was accessed, final record count, the NDB assessment and its date, any OAIC or individual notifications, and any customer notifications or complaints.
- Add pre-Completion covenants that the Seller procures completion of the investigation (we should consider requiring an independent forensic provider), with Buyer review of notifications and regulator correspondence.
- Add a **specific indemnity** for all loss from the incident, including regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully indemnifiable, notification and remediation costs, customer claims and contractual liabilities. It should sit outside the cap and thresholds and have a time limit of at least 3 to 4 years.
- Consider a retention or escrow amount.
- Add a warranty that, other than DD-006 as specifically disclosed, there has been no data breach and the Company complies with privacy law.

### 3.6 Sandbar renewals of AUD 330k (DD-008, DD-011)
**Facts:** There are three "related" renewals of AUD 110k each, which the letter asks to be "read together for timing/scope". The letter does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Seller position:** Ordinary-course operating costs.

**Why it hurts us:** Three identical related renewals look like a single commitment split into parts. That pattern can bring each one under internal approval limits, conduct-of-business covenant thresholds, or the de minimis. If they were entered into recently, in contemplation of sale, or above historical run-rate, they shift cost to us post-Completion.

**Push back:**
- Ask for the dates, terms, termination rights, prior-year comparatives, whether Sandbar is a related party of the Seller, and whether amounts are prepaid or accrued.
- Depending on the answers:
  - treat any non-ordinary-course element as Debt or a working-capital liability, or as Leakage if a locked box applies;
  - obtain a covenant that no further renewal is made without Buyer consent; and
  - confirm the aggregation rule (see 2.4) captures related commitments.

### 3.7 Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
The Seller's letter says these documents do not require consent. Those are the Seller's characterisations only. DD-009 restricts *assignment*; a share sale is normally not an assignment, but some clauses deem a change of control to be one.

**Action:**
- Our counsel should confirm independently.
- Require any DD-007 notification to be given in the required form and time, as a Completion deliverable or covenant.
- Add a warranty that no material contract or lease contains a change-of-control consent, termination or variation right other than those specifically listed.

### 3.8 Title (DD-012)
**Seller position:** Title is evidenced by the share register.

**Why it hurts us:** The register is evidence, not conclusive proof. The Seller's own letter (DL 10) notes we have not verified it.

**Push back and diligence:**
- Reconcile the register against ASIC records, allotment and transfer history, board minutes, the constitution and any shareholder agreement.
- Confirm there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs, ESOP awards or pre-emptive rights.
- Run PPSR searches against the Seller and the Company for any security over the shares.
- At Completion, require share certificates or lost-certificate indemnities, signed transfers, and waivers of pre-emptive rights.
- Treat title and capital structure warranties as fundamental (see 2.1).

### 3.9 Tax and IP warranties
**Seller position:** "Settled under the general regime."

**Push back:**
- Tax should be dealt with through a **dollar-for-dollar tax indemnity or covenant** for pre-Completion tax. It should be capped at 100% of the price, outside the thresholds, and have a time limit that runs past the ATO amendment period, typically statute-barred date plus a buffer, often 5 to 7 years in practice.
- It should cover the DD-005 on-costs.
- Given that Paperbark's value lies in its IP and the known Ironquay gap, IP ownership warranties should have at least a longer time limit and a higher cap than general warranties, or be treated as fundamental.

---

## 4. Security for recovery
Harbourglass is presumably an investment vehicle and may distribute proceeds quickly after Completion. Uncapped indemnities are worth little against an empty seller.

**Seek:**
- A **retention or escrow** sized to the specific indemnities, particularly Ironquay and DD-006, and possibly Bluefen. It should be released on agreed milestones.
- Alternatively, or as well, a parent or fund guarantee, or a covenant restricting distributions.

---

## 5. Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Seller position | Buyer response |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fundamental warranties | 20% cap / 18 months | 100% cap; 6–7 years; no thresholds |
| 2 | Default limitation rule | Applies to all Claims | Reverse; limitations apply to general warranties only |
| 3 | Limitations / non-reliance / exclusive remedy | All Claims of any nature | Carve out fraud, indemnities, tax, leakage, covenants, equitable relief |
| 4 | Basket / de minimis | AUD 250k deductible; AUD 25k | Tipping basket of about AUD 120k; de minimis AUD 10–15k; aggregate related claims |
| 5 | General cap | 20% | Depends on W&I; if none, 30–50% |
| 6 | Disclosure | Whole data room + public records | Fair, specific disclosure only; no qualification of fundamentals, tax or indemnities |
| 7 | Buyer knowledge (8.3) | Actual + constructive bar | Delete; pro-sandbagging clause |
| 8 | Disclosure currency | As at 22 Sept | Current bring-down; updates do not cure without consent |
| 9 | Bluefen (~30% revenue) | Reasonable endeavours; any written consent | CP: unconditional consent, cl 11.3 conditions satisfied, Buyer-only waiver, sunset; stronger endeavours |
| 10 | Riverlark (AUD 3.2m) | Release after Completion | Payoff letter; paid from funds flow; releases and PPSR discharges at Completion |
| 11 | DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420k + on-costs) | Off funds flow | Deduct as Transaction Costs incl. tax/super/on-costs; pay via payroll; indemnity |
| 12 | Ironquay IP | SOW3-payment indemnity only | Payment evidence + confirmatory assignment at Completion; broad IP indemnity outside cap |
| 13 | DD-006 privacy incident | "Not material" | Urgent update on NDB assessment; investigation covenants; specific indemnity; retention |
| 14 | Sandbar (AUD 330k) | Ordinary course | Full information; Debt/Leakage treatment if not ordinary course; consent covenant |
| 15 | Lease / Mossvale | No consent required | Independent review; notifications at Completion; change-of-control warranty |
| 16 | Title | Share register | Full title diligence; fundamental warranty; Completion deliverables |
| 17 | Tax / IP | General regime | Tax indemnity (100%, past amendment period); enhanced IP warranties |
| 18 | Recovery security | None | Retention/escrow and/or guarantor |

**Suggested priority order for the mark-up:**
1. The knowledge, disclosure and limitations cluster (items 2–3, 6–7), because without it nothing else is recoverable.
2. Riverlark and the DD-005 bonuses (price integrity).
3. Bluefen (value).
4. DD-006 and Ironquay (specific indemnities and retention).
5. Fundamental, tax and title.
6. Thresholds, cap and the remaining items.

**Immediate information requests to the Seller:**
- Current DD-006 status, including the NDB assessment.
- Bluefen correspondence and the cl 11.3 conditions.
- A Riverlark payoff figure.
- Ironquay payment status.
- Sandbar contract details and dates.
- A bonus on-cost calculation.
- Whether W&I is proposed.

I'd recommend local NSW counsel confirm the privacy, tax and limitation-period points before the mark-up goes out.

- Make non-reliance operate only in respect of statements *outside* the Warranties, Disclosure Letter and Transaction Documents.

### 2.4 Cap (20% / AUD 4.8m) and thresholds (AUD 25k de minimis; AUD 250k deductible basket)
**Why it hurts us:**
- The basket is a *deductible*. We absorb the first AUD 250k even when it is exceeded.
- There is no aggregation of related claims. This matters directly: the three Sandbar renewals of AUD 110k each, or a series of privacy-related claims, should be counted together.
- The 20% cap is within market range only if a W&I policy sits above it. If there is no W&I, it is light for a business with these known issues.

**Push back:**
- Make the basket a **tipping** basket, so that once it is exceeded the full amount is recoverable from the first dollar.
- Reduce the basket to around 0.5% of the price (AUD 120k) and the de minimis to around AUD 10k to 15k.
- Add an express rule that claims arising from the same or related facts aggregate for the de minimis.
- On the cap, confirm whether W&I is being placed:
  - If yes, we can trade on the general cap, but specific indemnities must sit outside the policy and the cap.
  - If no, seek 30% to 50% for general warranties.

### 2.5 General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Schedule 7; DL 1.1–1.2)
**Why it hurts us:** Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in" the data room shifts the whole diligence risk onto us. The words "referred to" also reach documents that are not even in the data room. Disclosing "publicly searchable corporate records" with no date or list is open-ended.

**Push back:**
- Delete general data room disclosure.
- Only matters **fairly disclosed** in the Disclosure Letter, with enough detail to let a buyer identify their nature, scope and financial effect, should qualify the Warranties.
- If any public records disclosure survives, limit it to specified ASIC and PPSR searches obtained on a stated date, with copies annexed.
- State that the Disclosure Letter does not qualify fundamental warranties, the tax covenant or specific indemnities.

### 2.6 Buyer knowledge / anti-sandbagging (cl 8.3)
**Why it hurts us:** It bars claims for anything we or our advisers "had knowledge" of, *including anything discoverable* from the data room or public records. This constructive-knowledge standard is the most damaging single clause. It would extinguish warranty claims for Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, DD-005, DD-006 and Sandbar, because each appears in the record.

**Push back:**
- Delete it.
- Replace with an express pro-sandbagging clause: the Buyer's rights are not affected by any investigation or knowledge, actual, constructive or imputed, other than matters fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter.
- At minimum, a fallback is the actual knowledge of named individuals, with no constructive knowledge and no adviser knowledge. That is still not ideal.

### 2.7 Disclosure Letter currency and updates
The Disclosure Letter speaks as at 22 September 2026, which is more than six weeks ago. Several matters, especially DD-006 and Bluefen, will have moved since.

**Push back:**
- The Seller must provide a current bring-down.
- Any update before Completion must not cure a breach of a Warranty repeated at Completion unless we consent.
- A material adverse update should give us a right to terminate.

## 3. Specific known-risk items

These matters are *known*. They therefore cannot be dealt with through warranties, given the knowledge clause and likely W&I exclusions. Each needs a condition, a completion deliverable, a price mechanism or a specific indemnity.

### 3.1 Bluefen change-control consent (DD-002; cl 3 / 6.3)
**Facts:** Bluefen generates about AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue, roughly 30%. Change of control requires consent under cl 11.2, subject to conditions in cl 11.3. There is no consent and no evidence the conditions are satisfied (DL 2).

**Seller position:** Reasonable endeavours; the condition is "satisfied" on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

**Why it hurts us:** Losing 30% of revenue would destroy much of the value we are paying for. A bare written consent that is itself conditional, or that imposes new terms such as repricing, a shorter term or extra termination rights, would satisfy the Seller's drafting but not protect us.

**Push back:**
- Make the condition precedent require a written, unconditional consent, or one on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably.
- Require evidence that all cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied, and a confirmation that no termination or variation right arises from the transaction.
- Make the condition waivable by the Buyer only.
- Raise the Seller's obligation to "all reasonable endeavours" or best endeavours. Give us rights to review and approve communications with Bluefen and to attend meetings.
- Include a sunset date with a Buyer termination right.
- Consider whether a price adjustment or earn-out is needed if Bluefen terminates or materially varies within an agreed period after Completion.

### 3.2 Riverlark facility of about AUD 3.2m (DD-003; cl 2 / 7)
**Facts:** The facility is outstanding, with a change-of-control provision at cl 8.1 and discharge at cl 9.2. It is not repaid and there is no discharge (DL 3).

**Seller position:** A release "to be provided following Completion".

**Why it hurts us:** The deal is debt-free/cash-free. A post-Completion release leaves security over the Company, and therefore over our asset, held by a lender we have no relationship with. The change of control may also trigger an event of default at Completion.

**Push back:**
- Treat the facility as Debt deducted from the price.
- Pay it directly from the Completion funds flow to Riverlark under a **payoff letter**. The letter should state the exact payout figure including interest, break costs and fees, and should be delivered before Completion.
- Make executed deeds of release and discharge, PPSR financing change statements and the return of title documents a Completion deliverable, not a post-Completion promise.
- Add an indemnity for any amount above the payoff figure.

### 3.3 DD-005 Completion bonuses of AUD 420k
**Facts:** Conditional Completion bonuses total AUD 420k. They are not in the funds flow, and the letter is silent on payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs (DL 5).

**Seller position:** A "matter for the Seller", not separately itemised.

**Why it hurts us:** These are liabilities of the Company triggered by the transaction. If the Seller does not pay them and they are not deducted, the Company, and in effect we, bear them after Completion. That is a leak from a debt-free/cash-free price. On-costs are likely to include PAYG withholding, payroll tax and probably superannuation guarantee, plus possibly workers' compensation premium, so the true cost is materially above AUD 420k.

**Push back:**
- Define these bonuses, together with all employer on-costs, as Transaction Costs or Debt deducted from the price.
- Show them as a separate line in the funds flow, paid through Company payroll at or immediately after Completion with correct withholding.
- Add an uncapped indemnity for any bonus or on-cost liability.
- Commercially, check whether the "continued employment" conditions create retention issues or claims if any recipient leaves.

### 3.4 Ironquay IP (DD-004, DD-010; cl 11.1)
**Facts:** Transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open. There is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment (DL 4).

**Seller position:** The existing indemnity, limited to the SOW3 payment, is adequate.

**Why it hurts us:** Until all fees are paid, the Company may not own IP that it presumably uses in its analytics product. Our exposure is not limited to AUD 180k. It includes infringement claims, loss of use, re-development cost and customer impact. The Seller's own letter also concedes the AUD 180k figure is not bank-verified, so the amount owed may differ.

**Push back:**
- Require, as a condition or Completion deliverable, either evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees (to be paid by the Seller or deducted from the price) or confirmation from Ironquay of the amount required.
- Require an executed **confirmatory IP assignment** from Ironquay of all SOW3 Project Materials.
- Expand the indemnity to cover all loss from any failure of the Company to own or have unrestricted use of the SOW3 materials, including third-party claims and remediation cost. It should sit outside the cap and thresholds.

### 3.5 DD-006 export / privacy incident
**Facts:** A download link was sent to an unintended external address. The file may contain about 1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, timestamps). Access, scope and notification requirements were undetermined as at 22 September. The letter does not characterise it as a confirmed breach.

**Seller position:** Preliminary and "not expected to be material".

**Why it hurts us:**
- Business contact details and activity data are still personal information under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth).
- Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must generally complete a reasonable assessment within 30 days. More than 30 days have passed since 22 September, so we need to know whether an assessment was completed and on what basis.
- If notification was required and not made, the Company has an ongoing regulatory compliance issue. Penalties under the amended Privacy Act can be significant.
- Customer contractual notification and indemnity obligations may also apply, including potentially to Bluefen.
- The Seller has no basis for its "not material" characterisation, and its own letter says the facts are not yet established.

**Push back:**
- Require an immediate update: forensic findings, whether the link was accessed, final record count, the NDB assessment and its date, any OAIC or individual notifications, and any customer notifications or complaints.
- Add pre-Completion covenants that the Seller procures completion of the investigation (we should consider requiring an independent forensic provider), with Buyer review of notifications and regulator correspondence.
- Add a **specific indemnity** for all loss from the incident, including regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully indemnifiable, notification and remediation costs, customer claims and contractual liabilities. It should sit outside the cap and thresholds and have a time limit of at least 3 to 4 years.
- Consider a retention or escrow amount.
- Add a warranty that, other than DD-006 as specifically disclosed, there has been no data breach and the Company complies with privacy law.

### 3.6 Sandbar renewals of AUD 330k (DD-008, DD-011)
**Facts:** There are three "related" renewals of AUD 110k each, which the letter asks to be "read together for timing/scope". The letter does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Seller position:** Ordinary-course operating costs.

**Why it hurts us:** Three identical related renewals look like a single commitment split into parts. That pattern can bring each one under internal approval limits, conduct-of-business covenant thresholds, or the de minimis. If they were entered into recently, in contemplation of sale, or above historical run-rate, they shift cost to us post-Completion.

**Push back:**
- Ask for the dates, terms, termination rights, prior-year comparatives, whether Sandbar is a related party of the Seller, and whether amounts are prepaid or accrued.
- Depending on the answers:
  - treat any non-ordinary-course element as Debt or a working-capital liability, or as Leakage if a locked box applies;
  - obtain a covenant that no further renewal is made without Buyer consent; and
  - confirm the aggregation rule (see 2.4) captures related commitments.

### 3.7 Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
The Seller's letter says these documents do not require consent. Those are the Seller's characterisations only. DD-009 restricts *assignment*; a share sale is normally not an assignment, but some clauses deem a change of control to be one.

**Action:**
- Our counsel should confirm independently.
- Require any DD-007 notification to be given in the required form and time, as a Completion deliverable or covenant.
- Add a warranty that no material contract or lease contains a change-of-control consent, termination or variation right other than those specifically listed.

### 3.8 Title (DD-012)
**Seller position:** Title is evidenced by the share register.

**Why it hurts us:** The register is evidence, not conclusive proof. The Seller's own letter (DL 10) notes we have not verified it.

**Push back and diligence:**
- Reconcile the register against ASIC records, allotment and transfer history, board minutes, the constitution and any shareholder agreement.
- Confirm there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs, ESOP awards or pre-emptive rights.
- Run PPSR searches against the Seller and the Company for any security over the shares.
- At Completion, require share certificates or lost-certificate indemnities, signed transfers, and waivers of pre-emptive rights.
- Treat title and capital structure warranties as fundamental (see 2.1).

### 3.9 Tax and IP warranties
**Seller position:** "Settled under the general regime."

**Push back:**
- Tax should be dealt with through a **dollar-for-dollar tax indemnity or covenant** for pre-Completion tax. It should be capped at 100% of the price, outside the thresholds, and have a time limit that runs past the ATO amendment period, typically statute-barred date plus a buffer, often 5 to 7 years in practice.
- It should cover the DD-005 on-costs.
- Given that Paperbark's value lies in its IP and the known Ironquay gap, IP ownership warranties should have at least a longer time limit and a higher cap than general warranties, or be treated as fundamental.

---

## 4. Security for recovery
Harbourglass is presumably an investment vehicle and may distribute proceeds quickly after Completion. Uncapped indemnities are worth little against an empty seller.

**Seek:**
- A **retention or escrow** sized to the specific indemnities, particularly Ironquay and DD-006, and possibly Bluefen. It should be released on agreed milestones.
- Alternatively, or as well, a parent or fund guarantee, or a covenant restricting distributions.

## 5. Summary of recommendations

| 2 | Default limitation rule | Applies to all Claims | Reverse; limitations apply to general warranties only |

| 10 | Riverlark (AUD 3.2m) | Release after Completion | Payoff letter; paid from funds flow; releases and PPSR discharges at Completion |
| 11 | DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420k + on-costs) | Off funds flow | Deduct as Transaction Costs incl. tax/super/on-costs; pay via payroll; indemnity |

**Suggested priority order for the mark-up:**

2. Riverlark and the DD-005 bonuses (price integrity).
3. Bluefen (value).
4. DD-006 and Ironquay (specific indemnities and retention).
5. Fundamental, tax and title.
6. Thresholds, cap and the remaining items.

**Immediate information requests to the Seller:**

- Bluefen correspondence and the cl 11.3 conditions.
- A Riverlark payoff figure.
- Ironquay payment status.
- Sandbar contract details and dates.
